evidence: store.py:79-84 builds a ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1); store.py:110 submits functools.partial(func,...) to it; store.py:112 awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future). In CPython, wrap_future on a concurrent Future uses _chain_future, whose _call_check_cancel calls source.cancel() when the asyncio destination is cancelled, which happens when the awaiting task is cancelled. concurrent.futures.Future.cancel() succeeds while PENDING, so the worker's set_running_or_notify_cancel returns False and the call never runs. Once RUNNING, cancel() returns False, so the call finishes. The CancelledError branch (113-116) re-raises and attaches _log_call_after_cancel to log the outcome, which is consistent with the docstring at 102-105. The rejection line about nested calls is a different defect and does not affect this claim.

store.py:111-116: on asyncio.CancelledError, run_memory_call attaches functools.partial(_log_call_after_cancel, name) via future.add_done_callback, then re-raises. _log_call_after_cancel (87-96): returns if future.cancelled() (so future.exception(), which would raise CancelledError on a cancelled future, is never reached); exc None -> logger.info naming the function; else logger.warning with exc_info=exc (an exception instance, valid for logging). concurrent.futures.Future.add_done_callback invokes the callback immediately in the calling thread if the future is already done/cancelled, so the already-completed case is logged too; otherwise it runs when the worker finishes. Absolute-claim trace: queued call cancelled -> wrap_future cancels the concurrent future -> callback fires immediately, cancelled() true -> nothing logged; matches. The rejection line (nested-call deadlock) is unrelated to this claim.

store.py:79-84 builds a single process-wide ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) behind a lock, so calls from any event loop go through one FIFO work queue: one at a time, in submit() order (store.py:110). Cancellation: asyncio.wrap_future chains the asyncio future to the concurrent Future, so cancelling the awaiting task calls Future.cancel(). In the window after the worker dequeues the item but before set_running_or_notify_cancel, the future is still PENDING, cancel() succeeds, and the worker's set_running_or_notify_cancel returns False so the call is dropped. Both transitions are under the future's lock, so there is no torn state. Once RUNNING, cancel() returns False and func runs to completion while later queue items wait behind the single worker. The except branch (store.py:113-116) adds _log_call_after_cancel (87-96): it returns silently if the future was cancelled (dropped), logs INFO on success and WARNING with exc_info on failure, and runs immediately if the future is already done. wrap_future copies the exception object from the concurrent future, so exceptions propagate unchanged. The rejection line (nested-call deadlock) concerns the separate docstring warning at lines 107-108; its cited callers are not part of this claim and were not needed. No counterexample found for two loops or the dequeue-then-cancel window.

store.py:79-84 builds a ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) (single process-wide worker, thread prefix sqllens-memory). run_memory_call (99-116) submits func to that executor and awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future). Crafted input: a function f running on the worker that does asyncio.run(run_memory_call(g)). The coroutine body runs in a fresh loop on the worker thread, g is queued behind f on the only worker, and the await on the future cannot complete until f returns, but f is blocked in asyncio.run waiting for g. So it waits forever; no timeout exists in the code. If the coroutine is only created and never run, nothing is submitted, so there is no nested call and the docstring does not claim anything about it. The docstring sentence (107-108) therefore matches the implementation. The rejection line (callers do not nest) is consistent with the head bytes and does not affect this accuracy claim.

store.py:79-84 builds a ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1), process-wide. run_memory_call (99-116) submits a concurrent Future and awaits asyncio.wrap_future. Cancelling the awaiting task cancels the wrapped concurrent Future. That succeeds only while the Future is still queued, so a queued call never runs. A started Future cannot be cancelled, so it runs to completion on the single worker. A later submission, such as clear_memories after the cancelled delete_memory, is queued behind it. server.py:594-595 and 623-624 call run_memory_call inside `async with admin_write_lock`. When the cancelled task unwinds, the lock is released, but the worker is still busy, so the next call waits. On CancelledError, line 115 adds _log_call_after_cancel with the func __qualname__. Lines 87-96 log INFO 'Memory store call <name> finished...' on success and WARNING with exc_info=exc (traceback) on failure, and skip a cancelled future. Absolute-claim input traced: delete cancelled mid-run, then clear_memories acquires the lock immediately. Its submit goes behind the running delete because max_workers=1. The doc at transport.md:120 matches the code. The nested-call rejection is unrelated to this claim.
